1:
Matthew Henry names two sins in the opening line: idolizing the Egyptians, as though the worshippers of false gods had the better interest in heaven, and slighting the God of Israel, who is not so much as consulted. Their kings had been forbidden to multiply horses, he adds, but they thought themselves wiser than their Bible. Charles Ellicott supplies the military attraction—the princes were reinforcing the weakest arm they had, a cavalry that an Assyrian officer could hardly mention without a smile. John Gill reads the opening as an exclamation rather than a curse, what poor foolish creatures are you, and lists what it cost: it broke the express command against returning there, showed how little the deliverance from that country was remembered, and exposed them to its idolatries. John Calvin gives the two reasons why the crime is reproved so severely—that confidence cannot rest in creatures and in God at once, since the eyes are withdrawn from him the moment they turn to them, and that the alliance was expressly forbidden, so that rebelliousness was added to misplaced trust. But he is careful with the principle. God does not disapprove of lawful remedies, any more than of bread; a man in danger who uses customary and lawful means, without denying God’s power, is not to be blamed. The fault is attachment to the outward means that leaves God unsought—and whatever draws the mind away from him, Calvin says, is our Egypt.

The second verse turns their own compliment against them. Gill points out that the God they disregarded is wiser than the politic Egyptians and wiser than themselves, wise enough to know all their schemes and to confound them. Ellicott hears sarcasm in it: the prophet ironically allows that the king’s counsellors were wise in their generation, and reminds them there might be some little wisdom in God too, and in the prophet by whom he spoke. Henry sharpens the same point—they take the trouble of a tedious journey when better advice was to be had by looking up, and if they will not court that wisdom to act for them they will find it acting against them. Calvin says the word wounds them deliberately, since men who shelter under craftiness and secret contrivance gain nothing but to provoke God further, a bad conscience always fleeing his judgment and seeking lurking-places; they had thought his threatenings empty bugbears and his foresight insufficient because he had not provided for their safety in their own way. John Wesley puts it plainly, that God is not inferior to the Egyptians in wisdom or strength, and glosses the help of the last clause as the helpers. Adam Clarke notes a singular reading, his word, in two manuscripts and two versions, and one that gives his ways.

On the third verse they converge. Calvin admits the statement looks like a truism—who ever imagined the Egyptians were not men?—and answers that the trouble is not doubt but practice, since men contrive as if they could settle for a hundred years everything they contrive; by flesh, he says, the prophet means weakness and frailty, and men are sent to learn from rottenness how frail they are. Henry draws the same lesson gently: it is good to remember that those we love and trust are but men, and not to forsake the rock of ages for broken reeds, or the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns; the horses, being flesh and not spirit, may be wearied by a long march or killed under their riders. Gill asks what use they could be with God against them, and Ellicott states the key-note, that a nation’s true strength is spiritual rather than material, so that without that condition the alliance would be fatal to helper and helped alike. Clarke makes the same identification in a line, the helper being Egypt and the helped Israel, and both falling together.
4:
Adam Clarke says the first simile is exactly in the manner of Homer, and prints the passage from the Iliad where the famished mountain lion attacks the thronged fold, undaunted though dogs and armed shepherds guard it. Charles Ellicott notices what is unusual in it: the lion is the symbol not of destruction but of protection, standing haughtily over prey it has made its own against the shepherds who would rob it. But the preposition he will not settle. Read one way God refuses to surrender Jerusalem, his peculiar possession; read another, the lion claims the city as his own prey, and God, using the invading armies as instruments, comes down to fight against it and will not have the Egyptian allies interfering with his chastisement. He leans to protection because of what follows, observing that the thought of supreme ownership contains both, since the city was his to protect or to chastise. John Calvin explains why the promise had to come here: if God forbade confidence in creatures and offered no assistance of his own, we might complain that he gave ground for despair, not consolation; every excuse is taken away by his engaging to be a faithful guardian. He adds that comparisons need not hold at every point, only be suitable to the subject. John Gill notes that the prophet had it directly from the Lord and could be depended on, and John Wesley that the help is pure grace, given to men who earned none.

The second simile reverses the temperature. Gill says the first expressed power, this one tenderness and speed: birds at a height keeping their eye on the nest and hurrying to hover over it against whatever would carry the young off—sharpened, he thinks, by the invader’s own boast of having found the riches of the peoples like a nest, with none to move a wing against him. Keil and Delitzsch read the change as the moment when the love enfolded within the wrath appears, and note the plural and the feminine adjective on a noun of common gender, turning leonine fierceness into maternal care. Ellicott says this picture comes from the tragedians as the other did from Homer, though there the point is the parents wailing over a plundered nest, whereas here the hovering eagle scaring off man and beast is the most vivid image of protection possible. Calvin adds that the birds almost kill themselves with hunger and shrink from no danger for their young, and sets beside it the eagle fluttering over her nest in the song of Moses and the hen gathering her chickens in the gospel: what Moses says God did, the prophet promises he will always do.

The last word of the verse draws Clarke’s best work. The common notion of a passing over, God skipping the marked houses, he thinks wrong, because the account of that night has two distinct agents: the destroying angel going through to smite, and the Lord keeping pace with him, who on seeing the token springs forward, throws himself in the way and covers the door so the destroyer cannot enter. The word elsewhere means to halt or limp or leap in a rude dance, and a lame man’s motion is a perpetual springing forward from the weaker leg onto the stronger; taken so, the bird spreading her wings before her young answers the figure exactly. He cites old Greek renderings supporting a going about and protecting, and Homer’s picture of a warrior screening his fallen brother behind his shield. Ellicott notes only that the word is the one used of the festival, and Keil and Delitzsch say the same, that the sparing of the doors from which the feast took its name would be repeated. Wesley reduces the verse to a sentence: the birds come from above and cannot be kept off; the destroying angel shall pass over the city.
6:
The call to turn is read as the heart of the message. Charles Ellicott makes it the sum and substance of the prophet’s teaching—with conversion all was hope, without it all was fear. John Gill spells out what they turn from and to: from the Egyptians they had courted and from idolatry and impiety, to the true worship and commands of God. Keil and Delitzsch place the call at the hinge of the chapter, addressed to the prophet’s contemporaries on the ground of a picture half terrible and half comforting, and strengthened by two motives drawn from the future: that idolatry would one day be seen in all its abomination and put away, and that the rescue would come from God and not from men. John Calvin disputes the construction. Some read it as a reason, return because you have multiplied revolts; he prefers a measure, return according as you have deeply revolted—meaning that however far they have sunk the door is not shut, and using the depth of the fall as a spur, so they should not aim at the half repentance men so often attempt. Those who need bringing back must first be given a painful conviction of guilt, since men who flatter themselves in their sins are furthest from pardon; but lest the heart despair, mercy must be held out beside the accusation, for the adversary aims at nothing but cutting us off from hope.

Matthew Henry hears the call in three voices, the rod, the sword, and the prophets interpreting the judgment, and finds the appeal to their parentage doing double duty: being children of Israel aggravates the revolt and encourages the return, for they have been backsliding children and yet children, so let them return and their backslidings shall be healed. He grants that the stain has gone deep into their nature and is not easily got out. Calvin takes the same name as a reproach rather than a compliment—they were degenerate sons who had left the faith of their fathers—while insisting that God had not forgotten the covenant made with those fathers. Adam Clarke notes that all the ancient versions put the verb of revolting in the second person rather than the third.

The casting away of the idols is the fruit that proves the root. Calvin says the earlier verse exhorted to repentance and this one points out its effects, since repentance is hidden in the heart and must be made known by works, as a tree shows its goodness by its fruit; the idols stand by a figure for the whole of conversion. He notices that they are silver and gold rather than wood and stone, because a man who has sincerely renounced superstition does not count the cost; and he has no patience with those who plead that the revenue is detestable but their living must come from somewhere—where conversion is real, what cannot be kept without dishonouring God goes at once. He observes too how readily the common people blame the priests, which is why the prophet directs them to their own hands. Henry adds three marks of the reformation: it is general, since every man begins with his own idols rather than his neighbour’s; thorough, since they part with what they were fondest of; and grounded on piety rather than policy, though he knows some read the verse only as a prediction that men will throw away in indignation what has failed them. Ellicott makes the same distinction of motive, that an earlier passage has the act springing from the terror of despair and this one from the repentance that is the ground of hope. Gill dates it to the moment they are convinced of the vanity of the idols; Clarke reports the difficulty of the last word, omitted by the Greek, supplied from other copies, and taken by one scholar as an epithet giving your sinful hands.
8:
The fall is by no human hand, and each of them says so differently. Keil and Delitzsch make it the second of the two motives for repentance—that the rescue would come from God alone, so that the very one they had fallen away from proves the only ground of confidence—and note that the prophet writes of a sword without the article, to suggest something unbounded and awful, drawn without human intervention; they reject the old Greek and Latin reading that puts a negative with the fleeing. Charles Ellicott observes that the original has no adjectives at all, only two nouns for man that are habitually opposed to each other, so that the point is simply that the whole work would be God’s and not man’s; the sword is that of divine judgment, perhaps of the destroying angel of the pestilence. Adam Clarke takes the two nouns historically instead: the camp lost upwards of a hundred and eighty thousand men in a night, and the king himself fell by the hands of his own sons—not mighty men, for they were no soldiers, and not mean men, for they were princes. John Wesley keeps to the angel, and glosses the discomfiting of the young men as a melting away, part killed and the hearts of the rest melting for fear.

John Calvin would read the opening conjunction as a mark of time, so that the enemy falls when their repentance is sincere; and he makes a rule of it: our obstinacy is why God adds evil to evil and doubles his strokes, so whoever wants the chastisement shortened should get himself reconciled. The deliverance is God’s own work: though no earthly power was visible, his secret power sufficed, and in delivering the city he exhibited spiritual redemption as in a picture, since he alone destroys our spiritual enemies too. On the young men Calvin notes that youth is fierce and impetuous for want of experience, so that the prophet names the very flower of the army to show how easily such fierceness melts. John Gill fixes the point that the destruction came neither in battle nor by the sword of the king of Judah or any of his generals, and dates it to the moment the people had repented and thrown their idols away.

The last verse turns on a single noun. Gill gives both readings—the king passing over in haste to Nineveh out of fear of the angel, or else his rock passing over for fear, meaning the men of valour in whom he trusted, who fled away. Ellicott decides for the second: the rock stands for the strength of Assyria, in a word different from the one used elsewhere of God, and the laws of parallelism make it the subject of the clause, answering to the princes in the next, which excludes the received version. Calvin keeps the king in flight to his fortress as to his nest, and adds that the officers whose business was to steady the ranks would not dare to hold them, fleeing instead from the standard; he thinks the prophet names himself God’s herald here so that no one should afterwards dispute the outcome or credit it to fortune. On the closing image the readings part. Ellicott takes the fire as the symbol of divine glory, giving light and warmth to the faithful and burning up the evil, and Wesley much the same, a fire to defend his people and consume their enemies. Calvin thinks the relative redundant and would render that God shall be a fire to him, with the Assyrian implied to be straw or chaff; he rejects the reading that refers the fire to the sacrifices as feeble and unnatural, and finds the point of its being kindled among his own people to be that persecution of the Church will not go unpunished.
